name: Overnight skin repair routine (retinol at night)

lead: This routine means applying retinol, a vitamin A derivative, in the evening, usually followed by a moisturiser. People use it for smoother skin, fewer fine lines and less rough, sun-damaged texture.

Retinol converts in skin to retinoic acid, which stimulates collagen and slows its breakdown. Clinical and histological improvement in fine wrinkles has been reported, though benefits fade after use stops. The better-studied retinoid is prescription tretinoin, with trials up to two years in photoaging. Evening use is linked to retinol's instability in light and oxygen and to retinoid-treated skin becoming more sun-sensitive; the overnight timing itself has not been tested separately.

paras: People apply a pea-sized layer to clean dry skin at night a few times a week at first, then follow with a moisturiser or barrier cream, and use sunscreen in the morning. Results typically build over months of regular use.
Redness, dryness and flaking are common, especially early on. Retinoids are generally avoided in pregnancy, and the EU and UK capped retinol concentrations in 2025. Skin can be more sun-sensitive.

angle.text: Retinol applied at night is converted in the skin to retinoic acid, which boosts collagen and helps fine lines, texture and sun damage look smoother. Retinoids have trials in photoaging; the overnight timing is mainly about the product's light sensitivity.

lead: An overnight skin repair routine is a practice of applying retinol, often alongside a moisturiser or barrier-supporting product, in the evening so that the skin is treated while the person sleeps. It is common in skincare communities and appearance-focused circles as a way to address fine lines, rough texture and sun damage, with the aim of smoother, more even-looking skin over weeks of repeated use.

Retinol is the alcohol form of vitamin A. The body converts retinol to retinal and then to retinoic acid, through which it acts by activating nuclear retinoic acid receptors that regulate gene expression [1]. It has been sold over the counter in cosmetics since 1984 [1]. Clinical and histological improvement in fine wrinkles and roughness of facial and neck skin has been reported, but benefits are not maintained after use stops [1]. The better-studied retinoid is prescription tretinoin, which has been studied for up to two years in photoaging [2].

Reasons given for night-time use include that retinol is chemically unstable and sensitive to light, oxygen and heat [1], and that retinoid-treated skin may become more sun-sensitive [2]. No study has shown that night application gives better results than daytime application.
infobox: EU and UK limits of 0.05% retinol equivalent in body lotion and 0.3% in other products from November 2025 [1]
Tretinoin (approved for acne in the US in 1971) [2]
Tretinoin contraindicated; high preformed vitamin A linked to birth defects [1][2]

paras: The routine usually combines cleansing, a retinoid, then a moisturiser. Supporters describe the moisturiser step as buffering irritation. Moisturisers work by slowing transepidermal water loss, with occlusives such as petrolatum reducing it substantially for hours [3].

Variants include applying retinol every second or third night while skin adjusts, a practice described for tretinoin in Wikipedia, which says applying every other or every third night can be considered if irritation occurs, then increasing frequency as tolerance builds, and that a non-comedogenic moisturiser can help [2]. The same source mentions waiting at least 20 minutes after washing and drying the face before application [2].

Retinol degrades with exposure to light, oxygen and heat, and is described as chemically unstable in topical formulations, which has prompted work on derivatives, antioxidants, chelating agents and lipid or nanoformulation systems to improve stability [1]. Topical retinoids are not classed as true photosensitisers, but users report greater sun sensitivity, thought to reflect a thinner stratum corneum and irritation [2]. These are the commonly cited reasons for evening application; there is no evidence that night timing improves efficacy.

Retinoic acid regulates gene expression via nuclear retinoic acid receptors [1]. Retinoids are described as stimulating collagen and slowing its breakdown, which is the basis for their use on photodamaged skin [4]. Very little retinol is absorbed systemically when applied topically [1]. Retinol is a precursor that must be converted to retinoic acid in the skin, which is the difference between it and prescription tretinoin, itself the all-trans isomer of retinoic acid [1][2].

Wikipedia's wrinkle article cites a 2022 clinical evidence review supporting retinoids for photodamage, with tretinoin and tazarotene the approved medical agents and retinol-type products regulated as cosmetics [4]. Topical tretinoin is described as the most extensively studied retinoid for photoaging, used for mild to severe photoaging in all skin types, with improvement typically taking several weeks or months, studied for up to two years and continued indefinitely or at lower concentration or frequency as maintenance [2].

The retinol article cites studies comparing retinol and retinoic acid on skin histology, molecular markers and clinical properties, and reviews of clinical efficacy and safety of retinoids for skin ageing; it does not report effect sizes [1].

Vitamin A was discovered in 1909 and retinol first synthesised in 1947 [1]. Tretinoin was patented in 1957 and approved for medical use in 1962, with James Fulton and Albert Kligman at the University of Pennsylvania co-developing its acne use in the 1960s, and FDA approval for acne followed in 1971 [2]. All-trans retinol entered over-the-counter cosmetics in 1984 [1], and EU Regulation 2024/996 set concentration limits for retinol in cosmetics that Wikipedia says took effect in the EU and UK in November 2025, with mandatory labelling [1].

Topical retinoids commonly cause redness, flaking, dryness and itching, sometimes called retinoid dermatitis [1][2]. Reducing frequency is a described way to manage irritation, and fine flaking can be gently exfoliated with a washcloth [2]. Retinoid use in pregnancy is contraindicated for tretinoin because of birth-defect risk, and high doses of preformed vitamin A are linked to birth defects; the FDA advises pregnant women to limit preformed vitamin A to no more than 5,000 IU per day [1][2].

Trials exist for topical retinoids in photoaging, chiefly tretinoin, with the longest lasting two years [2]. Retinol itself has been examined for fine wrinkles and roughness of the face and neck, with improvement that is not maintained after use stops [1]. No studies found that specifically compare nighttime versus daytime retinol application or test a branded overnight repair routine as a whole.

timeline.event: EU and UK concentration limits for retinol take effect (November) [1].
